title: The horse sacrifice as the cosmos (1.1)
hook: the Brihadaranyaka, the great forest teaching, opens by turning a king's horse sacrifice into the whole universe: the dawn is its head
tomorrow: in the beginning there was nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, after a hundred and one years, Indra learned the self is the one who sees through the eye. That closed the Chandogya.
screen: `INDRA RETURNS AGAIN — THE ONE WHO SEES THROUGH THE EYE.`

segments.voice: A king's horse, turned loose under guard. That's how tradition describes the start of the ashvamedha, the royal horse sacrifice. The horse wandered, the accounts say, for a year, and the lands it crossed were claimed for the king unless someone fought to stop it. Then came the sacrifice itself. And with this horse, a new Upanishad begins: the Brihadaranyaka. Not with the ritual's rules, though, or its costs. With a vision.
screen: `THE KING'S HORSE, FREE FOR A YEAR.` → `WHEREVER IT WALKS, THE KING CLAIMS.` → `NOT RULES. A VISION.`

segments.voice: Its first words, in Sanskrit, are usha va ashvasya medhyasya shirah. The dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse. Then it keeps going, part by part. The sun is its eye. The wind, its breath. The universal fire, its open mouth. The year is its body. The sky is its back, the air between earth and sky its belly. The stars are its bones, the clouds its flesh, the rivers its entrails, the plants and trees its hair. When it yawns, that's lightning. When it shakes itself, thunder. When it makes water, rain. And its neighing is speech. Read slowly, it's a portrait of the whole world in the shape of one animal. You've seen this move before. The Chandogya took the priest's song and found om inside it. Now the Brihadaranyaka takes a king's great ritual and says: look up. The real horse is already here. Dawn breaks across its head every morning. Its breath is the wind on your face. Some teachers take the passage as a meditation that lets anyone, not only a king, take part in the sacrifice by seeing the world as the horse. Brihadaranyaka means the great forest teaching. It belongs to the White Yajur Veda, and it was taught, tradition says, in the forest, away from the village. In the coming weeks it brings us to Yajnavalkya, and to the philosopher Gargi. But it starts here: at sunrise, with a horse the size of the sky.
screen: `USHA VA ASHVASYA MEDHYASYA SHIRAH.` · `SUN ITS EYE, WIND ITS BREATH.` · `THE REAL HORSE IS ALREADY HERE.` · `THE GREAT FOREST TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE DAWN IS ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Picture the sky at dawn, the first light along the horizon: its head. Feel the air on your skin as its breath, and let the clouds, the rivers you know and the trees outside take their places as its flesh, its entrails, its hair. Breathe slowly, and let the whole world feel like one living body, with you somewhere inside it.
Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice. The Brihadaranyaka opens by seeing the sacrificial horse as the universe: the dawn its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath.
Your line: the dawn is its head. Tomorrow, a stranger first sentence: in the beginning, nothing. See you then.

screen: `DAY 360 COUNTS.` → `THE BRIHADARANYAKA, OPENED.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE BEGINNING THERE WAS NOTHING.`

howItsDone: The ashvamedha is rarely if ever performed today, but the Brihadaranyaka is studied in Vedic schools of the White Yajur Veda and by Vedanta students, and its opening is often read as a meditation on the world as one sacred body.

original.note: Sanskrit aśvamedha: aśva, horse, + medha, sacrifice. the royal horse sacrifice.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient ritual about horses.
what it means: the grandest ritual turned inside out: the universe itself is the sacrificial horse, the dawn its head.
what a scholar hears: Brihadaranyaka 1.1.1; the Upanishad forms the closing part of the Shatapatha Brahmana of the White (Shukla) Yajur Veda.

chat.says: Why would an Upanishad start by describing a horse as the whole universe?
options: It turns a king's ritual into a vision: dawn its head, sun its eye, wind its breath.
It's a rulebook telling kings exactly how to perform the horse sacrifice.
It's praising the king's horse for winning him so many new lands.
chat.meaning: The Brihadaranyaka skips the ritual's rules and sees the horse as the world: the dawn its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath.
